newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says Burundi army killed at least 1,000.
newsitem.headline: UN says Burundi army killed at least 1,000.

text.p: Burundi's mainly Tutsi army, which grabbed power in a coup last year, has killed at least 1,000 people since the start of December, the United Nations said on Wednesday.

The U.N. human rights office, issuing evidence of the killings in the seven weeks to January 21, said they marked a new escalation in violence in Burundi's three-year guerrilla war between the army and rebels of the Hutu majority.
In a statement, it said Hutu rebels who are also accused of massacres of civilians in the increasingly dirty war were responsible for the killing of 58 people in the same period.
Worsening violence was accompanied by an army policy of forceful relocation of Hutu peasants and increasing use of mines by the warring sides, the Geneva-based U.N. body said.
The latest killings come on top of army massacres of more than 1,100 majority Hutus in October and November in the tiny central African country, according to human rights observers.
"The human rights situation in Burundi was characterised by a new and more serious outburst of violence and military operations in the reporting period," the statement said.
In the worst massacre on December 2-3, U.N. observers said troops killed about 700 people in northern Kayanza region.
In other big massacres, 121 people were killed on December 13 in rural areas of the capital Bujumbura, 75 people in southern Bururi region and at least 150 in separate incidents elsewhere.

The army routinely denies killing Hutus and blames rebels for the massacres. Tutsis are outnumbered four-to-one in Burundi and many fear they will perish unless they retain full control of the army and block real power-sharing with Hutus.

U.N. human rights observers said they were having increasing difficulty in investigating massacres because of worsening insecurity, which has made large swathes of the mountainous country no-go areas for foreign relief workers.
"A big majority of incidents are extrajudiciary executions, suspicious murders and massacres in the interior. But the mission is conscious that it is not informed of all of them."

The U.N. report made no mention of a slaughter of 400 civilians in the northwestern province of Muramvya on January 5 by troops and displaced Tutsis armed with machetes and clubs, reported by eyewitnesses and denied by the army.
Human rights observers said thousands of peasants, mainly Hutus, were forced out of their homes in the hills by the army and gathered in camps now housing more than 100,000 people.
Displaced Hutu villagers no longer had freedom of movement and access to health services, they said.
Diplomats and aid workers say the pace of massacres has picked up since the army grabbed power in a coup in July, prompting regional sanctions against Burundi to force a return to civilian rule.

The U.N. says the army has also killed hundreds of Hutu refugees who returned home reluctantly from eastern Zaire after a Tutsi rebellion late in 1996, in addition to 126 Hutus expelled from Tanzania who were killed earlier in January.
